translation: The boundless sea noise didn't stop for a minute.
It surged with long waves, sometimes intensifying, sometimes subsiding.
The wind would start to rustle in the bare trees, then fall silent, much like myself listening to the flow of the night.
But he did not leave, he was still here.
I knew this from the smell of wet pebbles and the barely audible shiver of a solitary plane tree leaf.
I had noticed this stubborn, bluish leaf during the day, but now, at night, it seemed to me a small living creature, my only wakeful friend.
Occasionally, gunshots could be heard from the darkness, from the city.
After every shot, the dogs barked for a long time.
Then a faint light flickered far out at sea and went out.
He made us look at these things more closely and for longer than we usually do, and discover many qualities in them that we had not noticed before.
In the yellow, porous stone, there were many tiny seashells firmly embedded into it.
A few flowers still remained on the bellflower bushes, sitting on their stiff stems like drenched and shriveled golden butterflies, patiently waiting for the sun.
But it only rarely showed through the fog as a blurred white spot and gave neither warmth nor shade.
Leaves lay scattered under the lone old plane tree with its lemon-yellow patches on the trunk, as if cut from dull green velvet.
Ants ran in a line through the iron gate, carrying their last supplies for winter to their underground storerooms, and under the anchor chain lived a small timid frog.
At night, someone on the other side of the river started waving a lantern and shouting in a drawn-out way.
I went out with my uncle.
Ilko to the shore.
The river roared.
The water was going over the dam in a cold waterfall.
It was late at night, dead silent, not a single star overhead.
The wild freshness of the thawed earth and the river was blowing in my face.
All the time, someone on the other shore was waving a lantern and shouting, but the words could not be made out over the noise of the river.
When the coffin was carried out onto the porch, I saw an old carriage on the other bank of the river, horses unharnessed and tied to it, and a small woman in black, my mother.
She stood motionless on the shore.
From there, she saw her father being carried out.
Then she sank to her knees and fell face down in the sand.
No, Grandfather replied.
That's true, we haven't met.
Ostap began to go blind.
He had then decided to get to Petersburg in order to see that woman before he went completely blind.
He got to the royal capital and found out that she had died, probably unable to bear the separation.
Ostap found her grave made of white marble in the cemetery, took one look, and his heart was torn apart on the stone lay his iron rose.
That woman had bequeathed to place a rose on her grave.
Forever.
And Ostap began to play the lyre and, likely, ended up dying on the road or in a market under a cart.
Amen!
On the other bank, Countess Branitsky's sacred forest rose up the slope.
The sun couldn't break through the thick greenery of this forest.
Only occasionally a solitary ray cut diagonally through the thicket, revealing to us the staggering vitality of vegetation.
Like sparkling specks of dust, little birds flew into this ray.
They were chasing each other with squeals and diving into the foliage as if it were green water.
I was filling a bucket with water from the pond, throwing grass into this water and waiting.
The red floats stood still in the water.
Then one of them would start to quiver, make gentle circles, suddenly dive or quickly swim to the side.
The father struck, the line tightened, the walnut rod bent into an arch, and splashing, bubbling and commotion began over the misty pond.
The water rippled, rocking the water lilies, water beetles hurriedly scurried in all directions, and finally a shimmering golden gleam appeared from the mysterious depths.
It was impossible to figure out what it was until father dragged a heavy crucian carp onto the trampled grass.
He lay on his side, catching his breath and moving his fins.
An astonishing scent of the underwater kingdom emanated from its scales.
Yasha was counting seconds to himself.
We knew that it was a seven-minute walk from Sturdza Lane to Landesman Sanatorium.
In the sanatorium, behind a high fence and iron gates, we always felt completely safe.
Especially if they didn't light any incense.
When we were passing by the gate, Yasha stumbled.
Later, when we recalled the incident on Sturdza Street, Yasha insisted that whenever you want to do something perfectly, you inevitably mess up over some trifling detail.
As for me, I thought to myself that Yasha's intolerable gait was to blame for everything.
But I kept quiet so as not to upset Yasha.
We crept along the alley.
I said to go on the side where the gateway is, stop before reaching it, listen carefully, and then quickly and silently dart past the gateway.
The calculation, in my opinion, was mathematically precise.
If there are people in the alley, they might not notice us.
However, if we walk on the opposite side from the driveway, we may be spotted from a distance.
I calculated that in the latter case we would be passing the dangerous alley, or rather, we would be within sight of people hiding in the alley five times longer.
And therefore, there will be five times more chances that we will be noticed.
In the morning, I was woken up by the hot sun beating against the white walls.
Red and yellow hollyhocks were swaying behind the open window.
Together with them, a nasturtium flower peeked into the room; a furry bee was sitting in it.
Frozen, I watched as she backed out angrily and extricated herself from the tight blossom.
Endless streams of light, gentle waves reflecting from the river, were racing across the ceiling.
The river was roaring right here, next to us.
